extracted.intended_audience: educated British political readers; members of clubs and societies; readers interested in the Constitution and the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative principles for composing political reflections/pamphlets evaluating revolutions and public conduct, aimed at a literate late-18th-century readership. Emphasizes prudence, institutional preservation, military discipline, rhetorical transparency, and the proper role of the pulpit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine liberty with stable institutions before praising it
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspend congratulations on a new liberty until one is informed "how it had been combined with government, with public force, with the discipline and obedience of armies, with the collection of an effective and well-distributed revenue, with morality and religion, with solidity and property, with peace and order, with civil and social manners."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that abstract liberty is insufficient; assess whether liberty is embedded in functioning institutions (law, revenue, military discipline, religion/morality, property rights, social order) before celebrating. He warns that premature flattery may corrupt both giver and receiver and that liberty without these supports is unlikely to be a lasting benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge political principles by circumstances, not abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Circumstances ... give in reality to every political principle its distinguishing color and discriminating effect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate political acts or doctrines in the metaphysical abstract; consider the concrete circumstances, historical context, and practical effects. A principle that is good in the abstract may be harmful in particular situations—prudence requires situational judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe how new collective power is used
rubrics_metrics.description: “Liberty, when men act in bodies, is power. Considerate people, before they declare themselves, will observe the use which is made of power,—and particularly of so trying a thing as new power in new persons.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When groups acquire power (e.g., newly-empowered assemblies or clubs), evaluate the character, principles, and temper of those who wield it and monitor initial uses of power rather than assuming benevolent ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing armies require unified command and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: An armed disciplined body is, in its essence, dangerous to liberty; armies cannot exist under a divided command. Better to put them under a single authority, with a simple oath of fidelity, and keep the whole under annual inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For safety and order, military forces must have clear, single authority and legal accountability. Multiple competing military authorities (e.g., crown army vs municipal army) breed mutiny, litigants, and instability. Regular inspection and unified obedience are essential safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating rival military bodies within the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting up, to balance the crown army, another army (a municipal army) creates a 'balance of armies, not of orders' and is likely to destroy order and invite insult and oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political reforms should not produce parallel armed forces under different authorities; such arrangements produce divided command, encourage mutiny, and undermine both liberty and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve constituent parts of the state when reforming
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer reparation, not ruin: "We took solid securities; we settled doubtful questions; we corrected anomalies in our law... In the stable, fundamental parts of our Constitution we made no revolution,—no, nor any alteration at all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing abuses, aim to correct anomalies and secure institutions rather than overthrowing the fundamental structure of the state. Reforms that preserve orders, privileges, property rules, legal and magistracy structures tend to produce stability and prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain military discipline during political change
rubrics_metrics.description: Military obedience changed its object in England's Revolution but 'military discipline was not for a moment interrupted in its principle. The troops were ready for war, but indisposed to mutiny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when armies shift allegiance or the political objective changes, preserving military discipline and chain of command prevents mutiny and preserves the army's function as an instrument of national defense rather than a tool of chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public political declarations require transparency of authorship and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A vote or resolution 'stands solely on authority' and the signatures of those who adopt it 'ought... to have been annexed' so the public can judge their number, character, and the value of their opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Societies, clubs, or committees that issue political addresses should identify signatories and be transparent about their composition and authority. Anonymous or ambiguous corporate-sounding resolutions risk appearing as stratagems and invite suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the pulpit to religious duties; avoid politicizing the church
rubrics_metrics.description: No sound ought to be heard in the church but the healing voice of Christian charity. 'Politics and the pulpit are terms that have little agreement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clergy and religious assemblies should refrain from partisan political agitation; mixing political agitation with religious preaching corrupts both and harms national tranquillity. The pulpit's proper role is spiritual and reconciliatory, not political mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of abstract doctrines used as political stratagems
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract principles (e.g., 'the king owes his crown to the choice of his people') may be advanced as a theory but reserved for later political use; equivocations and slippery constructions are used to make dangerous doctrines more palatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the plain meaning and practical tendency of political doctrines rather than accepting qualified or equivocal formulations; beware of doctrines presented as harmless theory that can be weaponized later to undermine existing constitutional securities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mixed constitutions to 'simple' governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple monarchy, simple aristocracy, simple democracy are 'imperfect or vicious; all were bad by themselves; the composition alone was good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional stability and good government derive from a balanced mixture of elements (monarchical, aristocratic, democratic) rather than pure forms. Writers and reformers should favor mixed institutions to avoid the vices of any single pure form.
